source_text: Ἐξῆν μὲν οὖν τοῦτο πρὸς αὐτοὺς μόνον εἰπόντας ἀπαλλαγῆναι. Ποῖον δὲ τοῦτο; Ὅτι εἰ μὲν ἀξιόπιστόν τινα νομίζεις εἶναι τὸν Χριστὸν, εἰκότως ταῦτα προβάλλῃ, καὶ ζητεῖς πρὸς ἡμᾶς· εἰ δὲ ἀπιστεῖς αὐτῷ, τίνος ἕνεκεν προβάλλῃ τὰς νομοθεσίας; Ἀλλ' ὅταν μὲν ἡμῶν κατηγορεῖν ἐθέλῃς, ἀξιόπιστος νομοθέτης ὁ Χριστὸς εἶναί σοι δοκεῖ· ὅταν δὲ αὐτὸν προσκυνεῖν δέῃ καὶ θαυμάζειν, οὐδεὶς οὐκέτι σοι λόγος τοῦ κοινοῦ τῆς οἰκουμένης Δεσπότου. βʹ. Πλὴν ἀλλ' ἵνα μὴ δι' ἀπορίαν ἀπολογίας τοῦτο λέγειν ἡμᾶς νομίζωσιν, ἐπ' αὐτὴν ἴωμεν λοιπὸν τῶν ζητουμένων τὴν λύσιν. Τίς οὖν ἡ λύσις ἔσται; Ἐὰν ἴδωμεν, τίσι, καὶ πότε, καὶ διὰ τί ταῦτα ἐπέταττεν ὁ Χριστός. Οὐ γὰρ ἁπλῶς αὐτὰ καθ' ἑαυτὰ τὰ λεγόμενα ἐξετάζειν χρὴ, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρόσωπον, καὶ καιρὸν, καὶ αἰτίαν, καὶ πάντα ταῦτα μετὰ ἀκριβείας δεῖ ἐρευνᾶσθαι. Εὑρήσομεν γὰρ ἀκριβῶς σκοποῦντες, ὅτι οὐ πᾶσι ταῦτα ἐπετέτακτο, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἀποστόλοις μόνοις, καὶ ἐκείνοις δὲ οὐ μέχρι παντὸς, ἀλλὰ μέχρι τινὸς διωρισμένου καιροῦ. Πόθεν τοῦτο δῆλον; Ἐξ αὐτῶν τῶν εἰρημένων· καλέσας γὰρ τοὺς δώδεκα μαθητὰς, εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Εἰς ὁδὸν ἐθνῶν μὴ ἀπέλθητε, καὶ εἰς πόλιν Σαμαρειτῶν μὴ εἰσέλθητε· πορεύεσθε δὲ μᾶλλον πρὸς τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἀπολωλότα οἴκου Ἰσραήλ· ἀσθενοῦντας θεραπεύετε, λεπροὺς καθαίρετε, δαιμόνια ἐκβάλλετε· δωρεὰν ἐλάβετε· δωρεὰν δότε· μὴ κτήσησθε χρυσὸν, μηδὲ ἄργυρον, μηδὲ χαλκὸν εἰς τὰς ζώνας ὑμῶν. Ὅρα Διδασκάλου σοφίαν, πῶς κοῦφον ἐποίησε τὸ ἐπίταγμα. Πρότερον γὰρ εἰπὼν, Ἀσθενοῦντας θεραπεύετε, λεπροὺς καθαίρετε, δαιμόνια ἐκβάλλετε, καὶ τὴν παρ' αὐτοῦ χάριν δαψιλῆ δοὺς αὐτοῖς, τότε ταῦτα ἐπέταξε, τῇ τῶν σημείων περιουσίᾳ ῥᾳδίαν καὶ κούφην ποιῶν τὴν πενίαν ἐκείνην. Οὐκ ἐντεῦθεν δὲ μόνον δῆλον, ὅτι αὐτοῖς μόνοις ταῦτα ἐπετέτακτο, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐξ ἑτέρων πολλῶν. Καὶ γὰρ τὰς παρθένους ἐκείνας διὰ τοῦτο ἐκόλασεν, ἐπειδὴ ἔλαιον οὐκ εἶχον ἐν ταῖς λαμπάσιν αὐτῶν· καὶ ἑτέροις ἐγκαλεῖ, ὅτι πεινῶντα αὐτὸν εἶδον, καὶ οὐκ ἔθρεψαν, διψῶντα, καὶ οὐκ ἐπότισαν. Τὸν τοίνυν οὐκ ἔχοντα χαλκὸν, οὐδὲ ὑποδήματα, ἀλλ' ἓν ἱμάτιον μόνον, πῶς δυνατὸν ἦν ἕτερον διαθρέψαι, πῶς γυμνὸν περιβαλεῖν, πῶς ἄστεγον εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν εἰσαγαγεῖν; Χωρὶς δὲ τούτων, καὶ ἑτέρωθεν αὐτὸ τοῦτο δῆλον ἔσται καὶ καταφανές. Προσελθόντος γάρ τινος καὶ εἰπόντος, Διδάσκαλε, τί ποιήσας ζωὴν αἰώνιον κληρονομήσω; ἐπειδὴ τὰ τοῦ νόμου κατέλεξεν ἅπαντα, ὁ δὲ περιεργαζόμενος, ἔλεγε· Ταῦτα πάντα ἐφυλαξάμην ἐκ νεότητός μου· τί ἔτι μοι ὑστερεῖ; λέγει πρὸς αὐτόν· Εἰ θέλεις τέλειος εἶναι, ὕπαγε, πώλησόν σου τὰ ὑπάρχοντα καὶ δὸς πτωχοῖς, καὶ δεῦρο, ἀκολούθει μοι. Καίτοι εἰ νόμος καὶ πρόσταγμα ἦν, τοῦτο πρῶτον ἐξαρχῆς εἰπεῖν ἔδει, καὶ νομοθετῆσαι, καὶ ἐν προστάγματος τάξει θεῖναι, ἀλλὰ μὴ ἐν συμβουλῇ καὶ παραινέσει αὐτὸ εἰσηγήσασθαι. Ὅταν μὲν γὰρ λέγῃ, Μὴ κτήσησθε χρυσὸν, μηδὲ ἄργυρον, ἐπιτάττων λέγει· ὅταν δὲ λέγῃ, Εἰ ἐθέλεις τέλειος εἶναι, συμβουλεύων καὶ παραινῶν λέγει. Οὐκ ἔστι δὲ ταὐτὸν συμβουλεύειν καὶ νομοθετεῖν. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ νομοθετῶν, ἐκ παντὸς τρόπου βούλεται τὸ ἐπιταττόμενον γίνεσθαι· ὁ δὲ συμβουλεύων καὶ παραινῶν καὶ τῇ γνώμῃ τοῦ ἀκούοντος ἐπιτρέπων τὴν αἵρεσιν τῶν λεγομένων, κύριον ποιεῖ τοῦ δέξασθαι καὶ μὴ τὸν ἀκροατήν.
thought_title: The command was temporary and for the apostles only
orientation: Chrysostom is answering the charge that Christians disobey Christ's command to possess nothing, and now begins to show that the command was given only to the apostles and only for a limited time.
pass_a_gloss: It was possible then, having said this to them alone, to be rid of the matter. What is this? That if you consider Christ to be someone trustworthy, you reasonably put these things forward, and you seek them against us; but if you disbelieve him, for what reason do you put forward the laws? But whenever you wish to accuse us, Christ seems to you to be a trustworthy lawgiver; but whenever it is necessary to worship him and marvel at him, no longer is there any word to you of the common Master of the inhabited world. But nevertheless, so that they may not think that we say this through lack of a defense, let us go now to the very solution of the questions. What then will the solution be? If we see to whom, and when, and why Christ commanded these things. For it is not necessary to examine simply the things said in themselves, but also person, and time, and cause, and all these things must be investigated with precision. For we will find, examining precisely, that these things had not been commanded to all, but to the apostles only, and to those not forever, but until a certain defined time. From where is this clear? From the very things said; for having called the twelve disciples, he said to them: Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter into a city of Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; heal the sick, cleanse lepers, cast out demons; freely you received; freely give; do not acquire gold, nor silver, nor bronze for your belts. See the wisdom of the Teacher, how he made the command light. For having first said, Heal the sick, cleanse lepers, cast out demons, and having given them his grace abundantly, then he commanded these things, making that poverty easy and light by the abundance of the signs. And not from this alone is it clear that these things had been commanded to them alone, but also from many other things. For also he punished those virgins for this reason, because they did not have oil in their lamps; and he accuses others, because they saw him hungry, and did not feed him, thirsty, and did not give him drink. The one then who does not have bronze, nor sandals, but one cloak only, how was it possible to feed another, how to clothe a naked one, how to bring a homeless one into the house? And apart from these things, also from another side this very thing will be clear and evident. For when someone came and said, Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? since he listed all the things of the law, but he, being officious, said: All these things I have kept from my youth; what do I still lack? he says to him: If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and come, follow me. And yet if it were a law and a command, it was necessary to say this first from the beginning, and to legislate it, and to place it in the rank of a command, but not to introduce it in counsel and exhortation. For whenever he says, Do not acquire gold, nor silver, he says it commanding; but whenever he says, If you wish to be perfect, he says it counseling and exhorting. And counseling and legislating are not the same thing. For the one legislating wishes by every means the thing commanded to happen; but the one counseling and exhorting also entrusts to the judgment of the hearer the choice of the things said, and makes the hearer master of accepting or not.

lemmas.gloss: to be rid of, to depart from

choices.why: The word means worthy of belief or trust; 'trustworthy' captures the sense of credibility Chrysostom is challenging the objector about.
The term is central to Chrysostom's distinction between Christ as commander and counselor; 'lawgiver' preserves the legislative force.
Chrysostom contrasts ἐπίταγμα with συμβουλή and παραίνεσις; 'command' keeps the imperative force distinct from advice.
The pair is technical in Chrysostom's argument, distinguishing non-binding advice from binding law; both terms are kept to preserve the distinction.
The participle describes the rich young man's over-eager, meddling response; 'officious' captures the slightly negative tone.
αἵρεσις here means the act of choosing or decision; 'choice' preserves the hearer's agency that Chrysostom emphasizes.

pass_b_english: Now, it would have been possible to be rid of them by saying just one thing. What is that? If you consider Christ trustworthy, then you are right to put these commands forward and press them against us; but if you do not believe in him, why do you put forward his laws? When you want to accuse us, Christ seems to you a trustworthy lawgiver; but when you ought to worship and admire him, you no longer have any regard for the common Lord of the world.

Still, so that they may not think we say this because we lack a defense, let us now go to the actual solution of the questions. What, then, will the solution be? If we see to whom, and when, and why Christ gave these commands. For we must not simply examine the words by themselves, but also the person, the occasion, the reason—all these things must be investigated with precision. If we look carefully, we will find that these commands were not given to everyone, but only to the apostles, and not to them forever, but only until a defined time.

How is this clear? From the very words spoken. For he called the twelve disciples and said to them: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans; go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Heal the sick, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received freely; give freely. Do not acquire gold, or silver, or copper for your belts” (Matthew 10:5-9). See the Teacher's wisdom, how he made the command light. For first he said, “Heal the sick, cleanse lepers, cast out demons,” and gave them his grace abundantly; then he commanded these things, making that poverty easy and light by the abundance of signs.

It is clear not only from this that these commands were given to them alone, but also from many other places. For he punished those virgins because they had no oil in their lamps (Matthew 25:1-13), and he accuses others because they saw him hungry and did not feed him, thirsty and did not give him drink (Matthew 25:42). How, then, could someone who had no copper, no sandals, but only one cloak, feed another person, clothe the naked, or bring the homeless into his house?

Apart from these, the same thing will be clear and evident from another direction. When someone came and said, “Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” and after he listed all the things of the law, the man, asking further, said, “I have kept all these from my youth; what do I still lack?” he says to him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:16-21). Yet if this were a law and a command, he should have said it first from the beginning, and made it a law, and placed it in the rank of a command—not introduced it as counsel and exhortation. For when he says, “Do not acquire gold or silver,” he speaks as one commanding; but when he says, “If you wish to be perfect,” he speaks as one counseling and exhorting. Counseling and legislating are not the same thing. The one who legislates wants what is commanded to happen by every means; but the one who counsels and exhorts also entrusts the choice of what is said to the judgment of the hearer, and makes the listener master of whether to accept it or not.

problems.source_quote: καὶ γὰρ τὰς παρθένους ἐκείνας διὰ τοῦτο ἐκόλασεν, ἐπειδὴ ἔλαιον οὐκ εἶχον ἐν ταῖς λαμπάσιν αὐτῶν
problems.why: The reference should be Matthew 25:8 or the parable as a whole, not verse 3. Verse 3 mentions the foolish virgins taking no oil, but the punishment occurs later in the parable.

problems.source_quote: μὴ κτήσησθε χρυσὸν, μηδὲ ἄργυρον, μηδὲ χαλκὸν εἰς τὰς ζώνας ὑμῶν
problems.why: The citation ends at v.9 but the quoted command about not acquiring gold continues into v.10.
problems.ruling: μὴ κτήσησθε...ζώνας ὑμῶν is Matthew 10:9, not 10:5-9; citation range is wrong.

problems.why: περιεργαζόμενος means 'inquiring further/curiously' or 'being meticulous,' not 'officious' (meddlesome/domineering). The young man is asking a follow-up question, not interfering.
problems.ruling: περιεργαζόμενος means 'searching carefully/inquiring further,' not 'officious' (meddlesome); mistranslates the young man's earnest question.

fixed: Matthew 25:3 corrected to Matthew 25:8: the source mentions the virgins being punished for having no oil, which occurs at verse 8.
Matthew 10:5-9 corrected to Matthew 10:5-10: the command about not acquiring gold continues into verse 10.
being officious corrected to asking further: περιεργαζόμενος means inquiring further, not meddlesome.

problems.quote: you have no further word about the common Lord of the world.
problems.source_quote: οὐδεὶς οὐκέτι σοι λόγος τοῦ κοινοῦ τῆς οἰκουμένης Δεσπότου.
problems.why: The Greek idiom οὐδεὶς σοι λόγος + genitive means "you have no regard/account for," not "you have no further word about."
problems.fix: you no longer have any regard for the common Lord of the world.
problems.ruling: οὐδεὶς σοι λόγος + genitive is idiom for no regard/account; not speech about Δεσπότης.

problems.quote: he punished those virgins because they had no oil in their lamps (Matthew 25:8)
problems.source_quote: τὰς παρθένους ἐκείνας διὰ τοῦτο ἐκόλασεν, ἐπειδὴ ἔλαιον οὐκ εἶχον ἐν ταῖς λαμπάσιν αὐτῶν
problems.why: Matthew 25:8 only has the foolish virgins asking for oil; their lack of oil and punishment span the parable (Matthew 25:1-13, specifically 25:3, 10-12).
problems.fix: he punished those virgins because they had no oil in their lamps (Matthew 25:1-13)
problems.ruling: 25:8 is oil-request dialogue; ἐκόλασεν and lacking oil are 25:3, 10–12, not 25:8.

wrong_scripture Matthew 25:8: fixed to (Matthew 25:1-13) — lack of oil in 25:3 and punishment in 25:10-12 span the parable, 25:8 alone is only the request for oil.
earlier `Matthew 25:3' -> `Matthew 25:8': superseded by fix to (Matthew 25:1-13), since neither verse alone covers lack and punishment.
earlier `(Matthew 10:5-9)' -> `(Matthew 10:5-10)': reverted to (Matthew 10:5-9) — source quotation ends at `μηδὲ χαλκὸν εἰς τὰς ζώνας ὑμῶν' (=v9), with no v10 journey-bag/coats/shoes content.
earlier `being officious' -> `asking further': left unchanged — `ὁ δὲ περιεργαζόμενος ἔλεγε' here is pressing inquiry (`what do I still lack?'), naturally rendered `asking further'.
